title: Two UK EMI failures land as Australia's AML reform consultation crisis deepens
summary: Two UK electronic money institutions enter special administration in 48 hours, raising CDD and safeguarding questions for APAC-connected firms. Meanwhile Australian industry associations fire a formal warning shot at AUSTRAC's reform consultation process. Plus the overdue HKMA STR thematic review obligation that will not wait.
script:
ALEX: Two firms in special administration in forty-eight hours. Not one, two. Both UK-authorised, both in the payments and investment space, and both landing in the same week that Australian industry associations are formally accusing their government of running an inadequate consultation process on AML reform. Jordan, I want to start with the UK pair because I think there is a read-across for APAC compliance leaders that is not obvious from the headlines.

JORDAN: I agree, but let me sharpen why. Jarvis Investment Management and ePayments Systems, which is the electronic money institution known as EPS, are not just a UK story. If any APAC-based firm had correspondent arrangements, payment rails, or client money sitting with either of these entities, the special administration freezes those flows immediately. That is not a theoretical risk. That is a Monday morning phone call.

ALEX: Right. Jarvis entered special administration on the fourteenth of October with Adam Stephens and Philip Hemming of S and W Partners appointed as joint special administrators. EPS followed on the fifteenth, with Mark Boast and Allister Manson of Opus Restructuring. Two separate insolvency teams, two separate regulatory sagas, landing in the same seventy-two hour window.

JORDAN: And the compliance question that matters most to our listeners is not the insolvency mechanics. It is the customer due diligence and safeguarding trail. For EPS specifically, being an FCA-authorised electronic money institution means there is a mandatory safeguarding obligation under the UK Payment Services Regulations. The administrators will be working through whether those obligations were met. If your firm is a creditor or a counterparty, you need to understand your exposure to the gap between what was safeguarded and what was actually held.

ALEX: I want to push back slightly on the framing that this is purely a UK problem. The FCA has supervisory relationships with APAC regulators through bilateral memoranda of understanding, and when an authorised firm fails with potential conduct concerns, those information-sharing channels get used. MAS, HKMA, AUSTRAC, all of them will be watching whether their supervised entities had material relationships with either firm.

JORDAN: That is fair, but I think you are front-running the regulatory response. Right now the immediate action is not to wait for a bilateral MOU to activate. If you are an MLRO at a payments firm or a digital bank with any historical counterparty relationship with EPS or Jarvis, you pull that exposure today. You map it. You document what due diligence you held on them as counterparties. And if there were customer funds flowing through those rails, you consider whether your own suspicious transaction reporting obligations are triggered by the circumstances of the failure.

ALEX: That is the right read. And the horizon question is whether APAC supervisors start looking more carefully at EMI counterparty risk in their own markets. The EPS failure in particular is a reminder that electronic money institution licensing does not guarantee operational or financial soundness.

JORDAN: Exactly. And I would add, if you have not stress-tested your payment chain for a single counterparty failure scenario recently, this is the week to do it.

ALEX: Moving on, the Australian story is a different kind of signal entirely. A coalition of thirty industry associations, co-signed by the Australian Banking Association, has sent a formal letter to the Australian government warning that consultation processes for complex legislative and regulatory reform are materially inadequate. This is a significant move. The Banking Association does not co-sign letters like this lightly.

JORDAN: It is significant, but I want to be honest about what it is not. It is not a challenge to the substance of AML and CTF reform. It is a challenge to process. The complaint is that the timeline for consultation on complex legislative change is too compressed for industry to engage meaningfully. And I have some sympathy for that, but I also think compliance leaders need to be careful not to read this as permission to slow-walk their own readiness.

ALEX: You are reading the regulator generously there. My reading is slightly different. When thirty industry bodies align on a process complaint, it usually signals that the substance of what is coming is more complex than the government has acknowledged publicly. The consultation complaint is often the polite version of "we do not yet understand what you are asking us to build."

JORDAN: That is a fair point. And the AUSTRAC obligation that is sitting in our board today reinforces it. The annual review and approval of the AML and CTF Program under Section 84 of the AML and CTF Act was due in August. If you are a regulated entity that has been tracking the reform debate and deferring your program refresh pending clarity, you are already behind. That is not a position you want to be in when AUSTRAC's examination calendar comes around.

ALEX: So the action for Australian compliance leaders is clear even if the regulatory horizon is not. Do not treat the industry consultation complaint as a pause signal. Treat it as a reason to document your current state thoroughly, so that when the reform requirements crystallise, you can demonstrate where you started.

JORDAN: Before we close, we have to name the HKMA obligation that is overdue and marked high priority. The Q4 2025 thematic review of STR narrative quality, which resulted in deficiency letters to roughly twenty-five percent of HKMA-supervised authorised institutions in early 2026, is still open for many firms. If your institution received one of those deficiency letters and has not formally closed the findings with documented remediation evidence, that is the single highest priority item on your desk this week.

ALEX: The HKMA does not re-open thematic reviews for sport. When a quarter of the AI population receives a deficiency letter, the follow-up examination cycle is not optional. The supervisor will be checking not just that you fixed the narrative template, but that the fixes translated into better quality STRs actually being filed.

JORDAN: And the December deadline for periodic CDD review of high-risk customers under Section 16 of the Anti-Money Laundering and Counter-Terrorist Financing Ordinance is ten weeks away. If your risk-rating refresh cycle has not started, it needs to start now.

ALEX: The through-line across all of today's stories is really the same one. Operational resilience in your counterparty chain, reform readiness before the final text lands, and remediation that goes to the board, not just the file. Busy week. The full obligation register and source links for everything we covered today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app.

JORDAN: If any of this felt like a list you were already carrying in your head without enough calendar space attached to it, that is the point. See you tomorrow.
